To form the plus-que-parfait: avoir / être in the imparfait + past participle.
To show the order of two past actions: what had happened earlier.

To tell the story of a first meeting with a family.

Saturday, 5 July, Iași. Ioana and Julien have arrived by train from Bucharest. Now they’re at the table with Elena, Dan (Ioana’s father, who knows a little French from school) and the grandmother, who only speaks Romanian. Ioana translates.
Julien, welcome to Iași! Did you have a good journey?
Very good, thank you. But I had never taken such a long train! Fourteen hours from Bucharest!
Ah, Romanian trains… That’s why we had suggested flying.
I was the one who had chosen the train, Dad. I wanted Julien to see the country.
Look at the table! Your grandmother made everything. She had started cooking three days before you arrived.
(in Romanian) Mulțumesc frumos, doamnă! (in French) It’s the only sentence I had learnt without Radu’s help.
Granny says she’s very touched. And that she had heard French people only eat cheese.
Julien, had you ever tasted sarmale?
Never! Ioana had told me about them, but I had never eaten any. They’re delicious!
Careful, Granny is asking if you want more sarmale. If you say yes, she’ll give you five more.
Then… (in Romanian) Mai pune-mi, te rog! (The whole table bursts out laughing.)
Who taught you that? It’s exactly what you shouldn’t say!
Radu! He had told me it meant “I’m not hungry any more”. If I had known…
Ha ha! My son… He did the same thing to me when I had tried to learn English.
Right, Julien. Don’t worry. My mother is delighted. She had never seen such a brave guest.
(in a whisper, to Ioana) Do you think I’ll be able to talk to your father alone this evening?
To my father? Why? (She looks at him, surprised.) You’ve been acting strangely since this morning…

“Zha-veh”: linked, without a pause. “Il avait” = “ee-la-veh”, “ils avaient” = “eel-za-veh” (with z; otherwise it sounds the same as “il avait”).
“Noo-zay-tyõ-par-tee”: compulsory liaison with z. Likewise “vous étiez” = “voo-zay-tyay”.
“Ay-mü”: masculine and feminine sound identical. The difference is only in writing.
“Bü-ka-rest”: that’s how Bucharest is said in French. Iași stays “Iași”, which French speakers pronounce roughly “yash”.
“See zha-veh sü”: three short words expressing regret. Said with a falling intonation.
It’s very easy if you know the passé composé: instead of the auxiliary in the present (j’ai, je suis), you put the auxiliary in the IMPARFAIT (j’avais, j’étais). The past participle stays the same.
The same verbs as in the passé composé take “être” (aller, venir, partir, arriver, naître, mourir… and reflexive verbs), with the same agreement: “Elle était déjà partie.”
2. When to use it: the past in the past

English has the same tense: the past perfect (“I had eaten”, “she had left”). In everyday speech English often skips it, but French uses it MUCH more consistently: whenever an action happened before another past action.
When we arrived, Granny had already prepared everything.
Julien had never eaten sarmale before that day.
Radu had told him it meant “I’m not hungry any more”.
… il l’a dite à la grand-mère.
… je suis arrivé à la gare.
Compare: “Quand je suis arrivé, le train est parti.” (it left the moment I arrived) vs “Quand je suis arrivé, le train était parti.” (it had already left; I missed the train!).
When you report what someone said, a passé composé in direct speech becomes a plus-que-parfait:
→ Radu said he had taught Julien three sentences.
Granny: “I’ve heard that French people eat cheese.”
“Si” + plus-que-parfait expresses a regret about the past, like “if I had…” in English. For now, learn it as an expression; you’ll do the full structure at B1.
If only I had learnt Romanian earlier!
Ah, if you had come with us…

She had never seen such a brave guest.
That evening, after dinner, the women had stayed in the kitchen. Elena and the grandmother were washing up, and Ioana was telling them about Lyon in Romanian, very fast, with big gestures.
Dan had taken two small glasses and an unlabelled bottle. He signalled to Julien to follow him onto the balcony.
The night was warm. Down in the courtyard, some children were still playing football. You could hear a radio somewhere, and dogs barking in the distance.
“Țuică,” said Dan, filling the glasses. “My cousin made it, in the countryside. Careful, it’s strong.”
Julien took a sip and coughed. Dan smiled. “The first time I drank Elena’s father’s țuică, I coughed for five minutes. He laughed all evening.”
Julien took a deep breath. He had rehearsed his sentence a hundred times on the train. But now he couldn’t remember it. So he thought of Hélène’s advice: no big speech.
“Monsieur… Dan… I love your daughter. I’d like to ask her to marry me. But first I wanted to ask for your blessing.”
Dan said nothing for a long moment. He was looking at the courtyard. Julien could feel his heart pounding. He had imagined this scene for weeks, but he had never imagined this silence.

At last Dan turned to him. “You know, in 1996 I was in exactly your place. On a balcony like this one, with Elena’s father. I was so scared that I had forgotten all my French, and all my Romanian too.”
“He poured me a second glass. Then a third. And after the third, he said yes.” Dan filled the glasses a second time, smiling.
Julien looked at his glass a little anxiously. So Karim had been right.

But Dan added, more seriously: “I’m not going to make you drink three glasses. I’ll tell you the truth. Since she’s known you, my daughter laughs on the phone. Before, she was alone over there, and her mother worried every evening. Now she has a family in Lyon. Thanks to you.”
“So… is that a yes?” “It’s a yes, Julien.” And Dan hugged him, like a son.

Then he lowered his voice. “Some advice, though. On Sunday we’re going to the grandmother’s village, near Iași. Behind the house there’s a hill with an old walnut tree. That’s where I had asked Elena to marry me. The view is magnificent at sunset.”

Julien thanked him. He was about to go in when Dan held him back by the arm. “Ah, and one last thing… The grandmother has already guessed everything. She saw the little blue box when she tidied your room. But don’t worry. She hasn’t said anything to Ioana. She had already kept my secret, thirty years ago.”

When Julien went back into the kitchen, Ioana looked at him curiously. “What did you talk about, my father and you?” Julien shrugged. “Țuică. And football.” Behind her, the grandmother gave him a little wink.
That night Julien slept very badly. But for once, it wasn’t because of the sarmale.

Reading text: The letter to Hélène
Julien writes a letter to Hélène from Iași. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Dear Hélène, I’m writing to you from Iași, as promised. We arrived on Saturday, after a fourteen-hour journey.
Ioana had warned me: “You’ll see, my family is a bit… intense.” She was right.
Her grandmother had been cooking for three days. There were twelve dishes on the table. I had never seen so much food in my life!
Do you remember the sentence Radu had taught me? I said it. Result: eight more sarmale. The whole family laughed for ten minutes.
Ioana’s father is very kind. He had learnt a little French at secondary school, thirty years ago. He had almost forgotten it, but he’s making a big effort.
For the moment, I haven’t spoken to him yet. You know what about. I’m waiting for the right moment.
The blue box is still hidden in my suitcase. Ioana hasn’t seen anything. Well, I think…
I think of you every Wednesday. Love to you, and love to Madame Bernard too. Julien
